outline.chapter_title: 1. The Refugee Suspension Order and the Litigation’s Procedural Path
outline.description: This chapter introduces the executive actions that triggered the case, identifies the parties and their claims, and traces the unusually fast procedural history from the district court’s preliminary injunctions to the Ninth Circuit’s interim stay order pending appeal.
subtopics: Executive Order 14163: suspension of refugee entry under USRAP
The related funding suspension under Executive Order 14169

The claims asserted: Refugee Act challenge to the suspension and APA challenges to the defunding
The district court’s February 25 oral injunction and February 28 written order
The government’s February 26 termination of cooperative agreements
The district court’s March 24 injunction requiring reinstatement of cooperative agreements
The government’s appeals and prior Ninth Circuit stay orders
The earlier carveout for refugees conditionally approved before January 20, 2025
The district court’s July 14 enforcement framework and magistrate oversight
The government’s emergency motion and the Ninth Circuit’s administrative stay
Why this order is interlocutory: merits opinion to follow, but immediate relief needed now

outline.chapter_title: 2. The Stay-Pending-Appeal Framework and the Court’s Interim Role
outline.description: This chapter explains the legal standard governing a stay pending appeal and shows how the Ninth Circuit uses that framework in an interim order that both preserves appellate control and previews its likely merits conclusions.
subtopics: The function of a stay pending appeal in federal appellate practice

The relationship between stay analysis, public interest, and separation-of-powers concerns
Why the panel denies the government’s July 17 emergency motion as moot after restructuring the stay

outline.chapter_title: 3. Presidential Power Over Refugee Entry: Why the Government Is Likely to Prevail on the Executive Order
outline.description: This chapter focuses on the part of the case concerning the President’s suspension of refugee admissions. It explains the statutory basis for the President’s action, the Ninth Circuit’s reliance on Trump v. Hawaii, and the court’s conclusion that the government is likely to succeed on this issue.
subtopics: 8 U.S.C. § 1182(f) and the President’s power to suspend entry of aliens or classes of aliens

How foreign affairs and national-interest considerations affect irreparable harm and public interest
Why the district court’s injunction against implementing the refugee-entry suspension is stayed
How this part of the order signals likely reversal or narrowing of the district court on the entry-suspension issue

outline.chapter_title: 4. The APA and the Statutory Duty to Provide Post-Admission Refugee Services
outline.description: This chapter explains the issue on which the panel parts company with the government: whether federal law requires continued reception and placement services for refugees already admitted to the United States. It details the statutory provisions the court reads as imposing mandatory obligations and connects that reading to the APA challenge.
subtopics: The distinction between suspending future refugee admissions and cutting off services for refugees already admitted
8 U.S.C. § 1522 as the statutory framework for domestic refugee resettlement assistance
Section 1522(a)(1)(A): the Director’s duties regarding employment, English training, cash assistance, and equal access
Section 1522(d)(2)(B): legal and financial responsibility for unaccompanied refugee children
Section 1522(e)(7)(A): alternative projects providing interim support, medical services, support services, and case management

outline.chapter_title: 5. The Modified Stay, the Ordered Relief, and Judge Lee’s Partial Dissent
outline.description: This chapter explains exactly what the Ninth Circuit ordered, how the panel tailored relief despite largely siding with the government on presidential authority, and how Judge Lee’s separate opinion frames the central interpretive dispute over § 1522.
